**Reduction.** Cell (1,1) has only two neighbors, so a Hamiltonian path must use both (1,1)-(1,2) and (1,1)-(2,1). The same holds for (3,1), which forces (2,1) to be a pass-through between (1,1) and (3,1). Column 1 therefore acts as a forced U-turn that joins (1,2) to (3,2). Column 10 does the same for (1,9) and (3,9), since (2,10) is not an endpoint. What remains is a Hamiltonian path from A to B in the 3×8 grid of columns 2–9, which also uses the two forced U-turn edges.

**Transfer-matrix count.** Scan the 8 columns left to right. The cut between columns has either one crossing (the path from A) or three crossings (the path from A plus one fragment whose two ends cross the cut). The width-3 and width-4 values were checked by direct enumeration. The sequence follows 2^w − 2, so for 3×10 the answer is 2^8 − 2 = 254.
